name: Frisette

card.summary: A short wig or band of curls worn on the forehead to add a curled fringe without styling one's own hair.
card.note: Worn as fashion and, by some Orthodox Jewish women, as a head covering.

quick.overview:
A frisette is a hairpiece, described as a short wig or a band of small curls, worn at the front of the hair to create a fringe. It gives a curled or styled fringe instantly.

Use is documented from the 1860s, and it features in 1910s-1920s hairstyling.
quick.how: The piece is placed at the forehead, often under a scarf or other covering, with the fringe arranged against the forehead or side-swept.
quick.risks: No health risks are documented. Fit and blending with natural hair are the practical concerns.

lead: A frisette is described as a short wig, usually of synthetic or blended hair, or a band of small curls worn on the forehead.[1][2] It lets wearers add a curled fringe without cutting or curling their own hair.
The word use for dressing the hair was established by 1867 in Harper's Bazaar.[1] Orthodox Jewish women wear frisettes as hair coverings, with bangs showing beneath a headscarf.[1]

chain: Hairpiece clipped or worn at hairline
angle.text: The piece provides a ready-made fringe, changing the look of the hairline without altering natural hair.

paras: Frisettes are short pieces with bangs arranged against the forehead or side-swept.[1]
Some Orthodox Jewish women wear a cropped frisette with bangs visible beneath a tichel.[1]

timeline.event: Use of the word for dressing the hair established.[1]
